brief.topic: Why seasons are not caused by Earth moving closer to the Sun
brief.desiredChange: Students can reject the distance misconception and explain how Earth's axial tilt changes Sun angle and daylight length to produce opposite seasons in the two hemispheres.

slides.title: Why summer is not ‘closer’
slides.purpose: Surface the familiar distance explanation and frame it as a mystery students can solve.
evidence: The claim that summer happens because Earth is closer to the Sun is a testable hypothesis.
slides.focalArtifact: A single provocative question: ‘Is summer when Earth is closer?’

slides.title: Make the idea predict
slides.purpose: Turn the distance misconception into a clear prediction before testing it.
evidence: If Earth–Sun distance were the main cause, the whole planet should respond in the same seasonal direction at the same time.

slides.title: Clue 1: January
slides.purpose: Challenge the distance idea with the timing of Earth's closest approach to the Sun.
evidence: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January.
Early January is winter in the Northern Hemisphere.

slides.title: Clue 2: opposite seasons
slides.purpose: Show that one shared Earth–Sun distance cannot explain simultaneous opposite seasons.
evidence: The Northern and Southern Hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same time.
slides.focalArtifact: A paired Northern Hemisphere/Southern Hemisphere seasonal comparison

slides.title: The distance idea fails both tests
slides.purpose: Combine the two contradictions and reject distance as the main cause of seasons.
evidence: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January.
The hemispheres have opposite seasons.
slides.focalArtifact: A two-check verdict on the distance hypothesis

slides.title: Meet the real cause: a tilted Earth
slides.purpose: Introduce Earth's axial tilt as the geometry that drives the seasons.
evidence: Earth's axial tilt is about 23.4 degrees.

slides.title: The tilt keeps its direction
slides.purpose: Explain how Earth's orientation makes one hemisphere tilt toward the Sun while the other tilts away during a season.
evidence: The seasonal mechanism requires the axis to retain its orientation as Earth travels around the Sun.
When one hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, the other tilts away.
slides.focalArtifact: The same-axis-direction idea across two orbital positions

slides.title: Tilt changes two things
slides.purpose: Preview the two consequences of tilt that control seasonal heating.
evidence: Summer brings a higher Sun angle.
Summer brings longer daylight.
slides.focalArtifact: A two-branch chain: Sun angle and daylight duration

slides.title: Effect 1: a higher Sun angle
slides.purpose: Explain why more direct sunlight produces stronger surface heating.
evidence: A higher Sun angle makes incoming light more direct.
The same incoming light is spread across a smaller surface area when it strikes more directly.
slides.focalArtifact: Equal light beams spread across unequal ground areas

slides.title: Effect 2: longer daylight
slides.purpose: Explain why a longer day gives sunlight more time to warm the surface.
evidence: Summer brings longer daylight.
More hours of daylight provide more time for solar energy to arrive.
slides.focalArtifact: A short-day versus long-day time comparison

slides.title: Put the summer chain together
slides.purpose: Assemble the full causal sequence from axial tilt to summer heating.
evidence: Tilt toward the Sun produces a higher Sun angle and longer daylight.
Those two effects increase seasonal heating.
slides.focalArtifact: Tilt toward → higher angle plus longer day → more heating → summer

slides.title: The other hemisphere gets the reverse
slides.purpose: Apply the same mechanism to explain simultaneous opposite seasons.
evidence: The hemispheres have opposite seasons.
When one hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, the other tilts away and receives the reverse angle-and-daylight effects.
slides.focalArtifact: Mirrored causal chains for the two hemispheres

slides.title: What distance can’t explain—but tilt can
slides.purpose: Compare the two models against the observations students now understand.
evidence: The distance idea conflicts with Earth's early-January closest approach.
The distance idea cannot explain opposite hemispheric seasons.
Axial tilt explains both Sun-angle and daylight changes in opposite hemispheres.

slides.title: Can you explain it in four moves?
slides.purpose: Give students a memorable structure for explaining the mechanism to someone else.
evidence: Reject distance using the January and hemisphere clues.
Name the approximately 23.4-degree axial tilt.
Describe higher Sun angle and longer daylight.
Connect the reversed effects to opposite seasons.

slides.title: Your turn: teach it back
slides.purpose: Prompt immediate retrieval practice and close on the causal idea students should remember.
evidence: The seasons are driven by tilt changing Sun angle and daylight, not by a seasonal change in Earth–Sun distance.
slides.focalArtifact: The closing line ‘Tilt changes angle and daylight—not Earth’s seasonal distance.’
